title: Tool Sandboxing & Permissions
summary: An agent's tools are its hands in the real world, and a compromised or confused agent will use them exactly as hard as you let it. Tool sandboxing and least privilege shrink the blast radius: run each tool with scoped credentials, prefer read-only access, allowlist the paths and domains it may touch, and isolate side effects behind a permission-checked wrapper so a single bad tool call can't delete a database or exfiltrate a file.
nestedConcepts: isolating side effects with a permission wrapper

subtopics.title: Least privilege: give a tool only what it needs
subtopics.explanation: Each tool should run with the narrowest set of capabilities that still lets it do its job, so a misused tool can only cause harm within that narrow scope. A file-reading tool has no business holding write or delete rights, and a lookup tool has no business holding an admin token. Least privilege is the single principle every other sandboxing technique in this topic is a concrete implementation of.
subtopics.example:
# BAD: one god-token handed to every tool
ADMIN_TOKEN = "sk-full-access"  # can read, write, delete anything

# GOOD: per-tool capability, scoped to the job
class ToolCaps:
    def __init__(self, can_read, can_write, root):
        self.can_read = can_read      # what the tool may do
        self.can_write = can_write
        self.root = root              # where it may do it

read_reports = ToolCaps(can_read=True, can_write=False, root="/data/reports")
# the summarizer tool literally cannot write or leave /data/reports

subtopics.title: Scoped, short-lived credentials
subtopics.explanation: Instead of embedding a broad, permanent API key in a tool, mint a credential scoped to the exact resource and action, with a short expiry, so a leaked or logged token is nearly worthless. The agent never sees the long-lived secret; it only ever holds a token that can do one small thing for a few minutes. Scoping and expiry turn a stolen credential from a catastrophe into a shrug, which is why it is the backbone of a safe tool layer.

subtopics.title: Read-only by default
subtopics.explanation: Most agent tools only need to observe the world, so make read-only the default and treat any write, delete, or state-changing capability as an explicit, audited exception. Defaulting to read-only means the dangerous verbs are the ones you have to consciously turn on, rather than the ones you have to remember to turn off. This inversion is what keeps a fast-moving codebase from accidentally shipping a tool with destructive powers it never needed.

subtopics.title: Allowlist paths and domains
subtopics.explanation: For tools that touch the filesystem or the network, define an explicit allowlist of directories and domains and reject everything else, because a denylist always misses a case. Resolve paths to their real absolute form first so tricks like '../../etc/passwd' or a symlink can't escape the sandbox, and match URLs against exact hosts rather than substrings. An allowlist is the difference between a tool that can read one folder and a tool that an injected instruction can turn into a file-exfiltration channel.
subtopics.example:
import os

ALLOWED_ROOT = os.path.realpath("/data/reports")

def safe_path(user_path: str) -> str:
    # resolve symlinks and '..' BEFORE checking
    resolved = os.path.realpath(user_path)
    if not resolved.startswith(ALLOWED_ROOT + os.sep):
        raise PermissionError(f"path escapes sandbox: {user_path}")
    return resolved

safe_path("/data/reports/q2.csv")          # ok
safe_path("/data/reports/../../etc/passwd") # PermissionError -- escape blocked

subtopics.title: Isolate side effects behind a permission wrapper
subtopics.explanation: Rather than trusting every tool to police itself, route all tool calls through a single wrapper that checks capabilities, validates arguments against the allowlist, and only then invokes the real function. Centralizing enforcement means the policy lives in one auditable place instead of being re-implemented (and forgotten) per tool. This permission-checked boundary is the concrete artifact that turns 'least privilege' from a slogan into code the agent physically cannot bypass.

foundations.overview: Tools are how an agent affects the world, so they are also how a hijacked or confused agent does damage. Sandboxing and least privilege attack this at the source: each tool runs with only the capabilities it truly needs, using credentials that are scoped to a single resource and action and that expire quickly. Read-only is the default, so destructive verbs are conscious exceptions rather than accidental defaults. Filesystem and network tools resolve and match their targets against an explicit allowlist — real absolute paths and exact domains — so path-traversal and exfiltration tricks fail. Finally, every tool call flows through one permission-checked wrapper that enforces these rules in a single auditable place the agent cannot route around. Together these techniques shrink the blast radius of any single bad call from 'catastrophe' to 'a blocked, logged error', which is the whole goal of agent safety at the tool layer.
foundations.formalDefinition: Tool sandboxing is the practice of executing an agent's tools inside a constrained environment where each tool is granted the minimum capabilities, credentials, and resource scope required for its function. Least privilege means those grants default to the smallest safe set (typically read-only, single-resource, short-lived credentials), and a permission layer intercepts every call to validate the action and its arguments against allowlists before invoking the underlying function.
foundations.whyItMatters: An agent's inputs are untrusted — a document, a web page, or a user message can carry an injected instruction — so you must assume the agent may at some point try to misuse a tool. If tools hold broad, long-lived power, one such moment can leak secrets, corrupt data, or spend money irreversibly. Sandboxing ensures that even a fully compromised agent is boxed into what its least-privileged tools allow.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each tool as a contractor you let into your house. You don't hand every contractor the master key; you give the painter a key to one room, for one afternoon, with instructions not to touch the safe. The permission wrapper is the front-desk guard who checks each contractor's badge and destination before opening any door — no badge, no entry, no exceptions.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Running code-execution tools in a locked-down container with no network and a scratch directory, giving a database tool a read-replica connection with SELECT-only grants, minting per-request S3 tokens scoped to one prefix, restricting a web-fetch tool to an allowlist of documentation domains, and wrapping every tool call in a policy check before it reaches the real API.
foundations.performanceImpact: Permission checks (capability lookups, path resolution, allowlist matching) are microseconds compared with a tool's own I/O or an LLM call, so the overhead is negligible. The larger cost is operational: minting scoped credentials and maintaining allowlists is engineering work, but it is dwarfed by the cost of a single unbounded incident.
commonUseCases: Sandboxing code-execution tools in a no-network container
Read-only database connections for lookup tools
Per-request, short-lived scoped credentials for cloud resources
Path/domain allowlists for filesystem and web-fetch tools

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the prompt tells the agent not to misuse a tool, that's enough.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Prompts are advisory and can be overridden by injection or confusion. Enforcement has to live in code — a permission wrapper the agent cannot talk its way past — not in instructions the model may ignore.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A denylist of dangerous paths/domains is a fine sandbox.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Denylists always miss a case (a new path, an encoded traversal, a lookalike domain). Least privilege uses an allowlist: everything is denied except an explicit, small set you resolved and verified.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Checking the string a user passed is enough to keep a file tool safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You must resolve the path to its real absolute form first, because '..' segments and symlinks can escape the sandbox before any naive prefix check runs.

codeLab.title: Build a least-privilege tool gateway
codeLab.instructions: Implement guard_call(tool_fn, caps, action, url=None) that enforces least privilege before running a network tool. It must (1) raise PermissionError if action is in {'write','delete','send'} and caps.can_write is False; (2) if a url is provided, raise PermissionError unless its host is in caps.allowed_domains (exact host match, not substring — parse the host with urllib); (3) otherwise call tool_fn(url=url) if url is given, else tool_fn(), and return its result. Complete the function so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
def fetch(url=None): return f"fetched {url}"
caps = ToolCaps(can_write=False, allowed_domains={"docs.example.com"})

# allowed read from an allowlisted domain
assert guard_call(fetch, caps, "read", url="https://docs.example.com/page") == "fetched https://docs.example.com/page"

# blocked: mutating action without write capability
try:
    guard_call(fetch, caps, "send", url="https://docs.example.com/page")
    raise AssertionError("should have raised")
except PermissionError:
    pass

# blocked: lookalike / non-allowlisted domain
try:
    guard_call(fetch, caps, "read", url="https://docs.example.com.evil.com/x")
    raise AssertionError("should have raised")
except PermissionError:
    pass
print("all tests passed")
hints: Check the capability gate first (mutating action + not can_write), then the domain gate, then invoke the tool.
Use urlparse(url).hostname to get the real host, and compare it with `in caps.allowed_domains` for an exact match.
A substring check like `'example.com' in url` is unsafe — 'docs.example.com.evil.com' would pass it; exact host equality does not.

Log tool calls but allow all of them
checkpoints.explanation: Least privilege means each tool gets only the capabilities, credentials, and resource scope required for its job, so a misused tool can only cause harm within that narrow scope.

checkpoints.prompt: This file tool tries to stay inside /data but still lets an attacker escape. What's wrong?
options: The check uses the raw string, so '..' segments (and symlinks) escape /data before the prefix is ever resolved
checkpoints.explanation: '/data/../etc/passwd' starts with '/data' but resolves to /etc/passwd. You must call os.path.realpath first to collapse '..' and symlinks, then check the resolved path against an allowlisted root.

checkpoints.prompt: Given MUTATING = {'write','delete'} and caps.can_write = False, what does this print?
checkpoints.code:
MUTATING = {"write", "delete"}
can_write = False
action = "delete"
print("blocked" if (action in MUTATING and not can_write) else "allowed")
checkpoints.explanation: 'delete' is a mutating action and can_write is False, so the guard condition is True and it prints 'blocked' — writes are opt-in, so the delete is denied.

theory.question: What does least privilege mean for an agent's tools, and how do you enforce it?
theory.directAnswer: It means every tool runs with the smallest set of capabilities, credentials, and resource scope needed for its job — read-only by default, single-resource scoped credentials that expire quickly — and you enforce it in code with a permission wrapper that checks the action and its arguments against allowlists before invoking the real function, never relying on the prompt.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Least privilege for tools is granting each tool only the minimum power required and executing every call through a constrained boundary that validates it first.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An agent's inputs are untrusted (documents, web pages, user text can carry injected instructions), so you must assume the agent may at some point try to misuse a tool; broad, long-lived tool power turns that moment into a serious incident.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You model per-tool capabilities (read/write, resource root), mint scoped short-lived credentials instead of embedding a god-token, default to read-only so destructive verbs are explicit exceptions, allowlist filesystem paths (after os.path.realpath) and network domains (exact host match), and route all calls through one wrapper that applies these checks.

theory.whyImportant: It is the primary control that shrinks the blast radius of a compromised or confused agent from a catastrophe to a blocked, logged error.
theory.realWorldExample: A code-execution tool runs inside a network-less container with only a scratch directory, and a database tool uses a read-replica connection with SELECT-only grants, so even a fully hijacked agent can neither reach the internet nor mutate production data.

followUps.question: Why not enforce the rules in the system prompt?
followUps.answer: Prompts are advisory and can be overridden by injection or model confusion. Enforcement must be in code the agent cannot talk its way past — the prompt is documentation, not a control.

followUps.question: Why prefer an allowlist over a denylist for paths and domains?
followUps.answer: Denylists inevitably miss a case (a new path, an encoded traversal, a lookalike domain). An allowlist denies everything except a small, explicitly verified set.

theory.question: How do scoped, short-lived credentials reduce risk compared with a long-lived API key embedded in a tool?
theory.directAnswer: A scoped, short-lived credential can perform only one action on one resource and expires in minutes, so if it leaks — via logs, an error message, or a compromised agent — the attacker gains almost nothing and only for a moment, whereas a leaked long-lived god-key grants broad, lasting access to everything.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Scoped credentials are tokens minted per request that encode a specific resource, a specific action, and a short expiry, rather than a broad standing secret.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Secrets leak in practice — into logs, traces, prompts, or the model's own output — and an agent's untrusted inputs raise the odds; the goal is to make each secret worth as little as possible if it escapes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A credential broker (e.g. STS-style token exchange or signed JWTs) issues a token bound to one resource and verb with a TTL of minutes; the agent never holds the long-lived root secret, and expiry plus scope cap what any single leaked token can do.

theory.whyImportant: It converts a leaked credential from a full breach into a near-non-event, which is essential because you cannot guarantee an agent-facing tool will never leak its token.
theory.realWorldExample: A reporting tool requests a token scoped to read one S3 prefix for 120 seconds per call; when that token later showed up in a debug log, it had already expired and could only ever have read one folder.

followUps.question: Where should the long-lived secret live instead?
followUps.answer: In a secrets manager or credential broker that the tool backend calls to mint scoped tokens; the agent and tool-facing layer never see the root secret.

followUps.question: What TTL is appropriate?
followUps.answer: As short as the operation allows — often seconds to a few minutes — long enough for one call plus retries, short enough that a leaked token is stale almost immediately.

scenario.question: Your agent has a file-summarizer tool and a web-fetch tool. A pentest shows a document with an injected instruction made the agent read /etc/passwd and POST it to an external host. How do you sandbox these tools so this can't happen?
scenario.directAnswer: Put both tools behind a permission wrapper enforcing least privilege: give the file tool read-only capability rooted at the documents directory and resolve every path with os.path.realpath against that allowlisted root; give the web tool an allowlist of exact domains and no write/POST capability at all; run the whole thing with scoped, short-lived credentials and a no-egress network posture except the allowlisted hosts.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A blast-radius-reduction exercise: the injection succeeded because the tools had more power and reach than their jobs required.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The file tool could resolve arbitrary paths and the web tool could reach arbitrary domains with a mutating verb, so a single injected instruction chained a local read into an external exfiltration.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Root the file tool at /data/docs and reject any realpath outside it (killing the traversal to /etc/passwd); restrict the web tool to an allowlist of documentation domains and strip its ability to POST; mint per-call scoped credentials; and centralize all checks in one wrapper so neither tool can be re-added without the gate.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the defense is architectural, not prompt-based: you remove the capability that made the exploit possible rather than asking the model not to use it.
scenario.realWorldExample: After rooting the file tool and allowlisting web domains, the same malicious document produced two blocked, logged PermissionErrors instead of a data leak, and the alert on those blocks flagged the poisoned document for review.

followUps.question: Why block the exfiltration domain instead of just the file read?
followUps.answer: Defense in depth — even if a future bug lets a sensitive read through, an egress allowlist means there is nowhere for the data to be sent, so both legs of the exploit are independently closed.

followUps.question: How would you detect this attempt going forward?
followUps.answer: Alert on PermissionError rates from the wrapper; a spike of path-escape or domain-deny errors is a strong signal that a document or input is trying to abuse the tools.

coding.question: Write a permission-checked wrapper factory that enforces read-only-by-default capability and a filesystem path allowlist before running a tool, raising PermissionError on any violation.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want one place that enforces policy, so I write a factory returning a wrapped tool. It first gates mutating actions on a can_write capability, then, for any path argument, resolves the path with os.path.realpath and requires it to sit under the allowlisted root before calling the real function. Resolving before checking is essential so '..' and symlinks can't escape; centralizing it means the raw tool is never exposed.
lineByLine: MUTATING lists the verbs that require an explicit write capability, so everything else is read-only by default.
safe_path resolves both the root and the requested path with realpath, collapsing '..' and symlinks before any comparison.
It then requires the resolved path to equal or sit under the allowlisted root, raising PermissionError otherwise.
make_permissioned returns a closure so policy (action, capability, root) is bound once and enforced on every call.
The wrapper checks the capability gate first, then rewrites the path argument through safe_path, then invokes the real tool.
The __main__ block shows an in-scope read succeeding and a traversal attempt being blocked before the tool runs.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the length of the path for realpath resolution and the prefix check.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the resolved path string; the wrapper itself holds only its bound policy.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to network tools?
followUps.answer: Add a domain allowlist check: parse the URL host with urlparse and require an exact match against an allowed_domains set, mirroring the path allowlist for the filesystem.

followUps.question: How do scoped credentials fit in?
followUps.answer: The wrapper can mint or attach a short-lived token scoped to the resolved resource and action just before calling tool_fn, so the tool never holds a broad standing secret.

keyTakeaways: Tools are how an agent affects the world, so a hijacked agent does damage exactly as far as its tools' privileges reach.
Apply least privilege: each tool gets only the capabilities, resource scope, and short-lived scoped credentials its job requires.
Default to read-only so destructive verbs (write, delete, send, pay) are conscious, audited exceptions rather than accidents.
Allowlist filesystem paths (after os.path.realpath) and network domains (exact host match) — never rely on a denylist.
Enforce all of this in one permission-checked wrapper the agent cannot bypass; the prompt is documentation, not a control.
